summary: This RFC introduces a series of specifications for fully supporting internationalized email addresses. Users should be able to use mailbox names in their own language and script. It describes the changes and protocol extensions needed across mail systems.

eli5.summary: Email addresses were once only for English letters. This starts a set of rules so people can use their own alphabets in their email names.

questions: can email addresses use non-ascii characters
subtitle: The framework for email addresses and headers written in the sender's own language and script, using UTF-8.

tldr.problem: Domain names can already be internationalized, but the local part of an email address is limited to a subset of 7-bit ASCII, so people cannot use mailbox names in their own scripts.
tldr.mechanism: A set of specifications adds an SMTP extension, SMTPUTF8, and lets email header fields carry UTF-8 directly, with matching changes to delivery status notifications, IMAP and POP.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is the overview for that set. It replaces the earlier experimental framework, drops in-transit downgrading, and obsoletes RFC 4952, RFC 5504 and RFC 5825.

today: RFC 6530 is a Proposed Standard from February 2012 that obsoletes RFC 4952, RFC 5504 and RFC 5825, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The detailed protocol work lives in the companion documents RFC 6531, RFC 6532 and RFC 6533.

sections.title: Why Email Addresses Need Internationalizing
sections.content:
An email address has two halves: the local part (the mailbox name) and the domain part. The domain part is already internationalized through IDNA, but the local part is not. Without these extensions the mailbox name is restricted to a subset of 7-bit ASCII as defined in RFC 5321.

MIME can carry non-ASCII data, and RFC 2047 encodes non-ASCII text in some header fields, but neither allows non-ASCII characters in the address itself. The only workaround is to put them in the display name, which is invisible in the message envelope and for many purposes is not part of the address at all.

This document replaces RFC 4952 and reflects issues identified since it was published.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mailbox that only accepts labels written in English letters. This RFC is the plan for letting people write their own names on the label.

sections.title: The Problem Statement
sections.content:
The RFC argues that internationalized domain names alone have little value until more of the identifiers around them are internationalized. Users prefer addresses that resemble names or initials, and unless the whole address can use familiar characters, email will be perceived as culturally unfriendly.

It also argues that patches are not enough. Changing only the SMTP envelope, the From:, To: and Cc: header fields, or having upgraded mail user agents decode a special coding, would leave a mix of implementations with different workarounds and confuse users. Instead it calls for a fully internationalized environment: header fields that can use the full range of Unicode, an SMTP extension for UTF-8 addressing and delivery, internationalized delivery notifications, and a requirement for the 8BITMIME extension so these can travel without a content-transfer-encoding.
sections.eli5: Fixing just one piece, like the town name on an address, is not enough. The whole address and everything that handles it has to understand the new letters.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms used across the document set.

  • An address is all-ASCII if every character is in the ASCII repertoire, and non-ASCII (an i18n-address) if any character is not. The umbrella term for the whole approach is SMTPUTF8.
  • An ASCII user only uses and can only generate ASCII addresses. An internationalized email user has a non-ASCII address or can generate non-ASCII recipient addresses. There is no such thing as an internationalized email user message.
  • A conventional message uses none of the extensions and strictly conforms to RFC 5322. An internationalized message uses one or more of the extensions and no longer conforms to the traditional specification.
  • The final delivery MTA is the SMTP server that controls the format of local parts and may inspect and interpret them.
sections.eli5: An address is either all plain English letters or it has at least one other letter. A message that uses the new features is a new kind of message that old mail programs may not understand.

sections.title: The Document Set
sections.content:
The specifications change both SMTP and the character encoding of message headers so that non-ASCII characters can be represented directly. The set includes:

  • An SMTP extension for internationalized addresses, RFC 6531.
  • A UTF-8 email header specification, RFC 6532, which essentially updates RFC 5322 so some header information can be expressed directly in UTF-8 when the SMTP extension is used.
  • Internationalized delivery and disposition notifications, RFC 6533.
  • Forthcoming documents for IMAP and POP support.

Conformance for transport and delivery requires implementing the SMTP extension and the UTF-8 header specification. A system that implements IMAP or POP must conform to the internationalized versions of those too.
sections.eli5: This RFC is the table of contents for a small book. Each chapter covers one piece: sending mail, the header labels, the failure notices, and picking up mail.

sections.title: The SMTPUTF8 Extension and UTF-8 Headers
sections.content:
The SMTPUTF8 SMTP extension permits UTF-8 strings in the local part and in domain names, permits selective use of UTF-8 in message headers, and requires the server to advertise 8BITMIME and the client to support 8-bit transmission. Unlike the earlier experiment, the client must now announce the SMTPUTF8 keyword when it needs the extension.

The design principles include:

  • An SMTP relay MUST either recognize the format via the ESMTP option or reject the message, or send a non-delivery notification, so the sender can make another plan. The same applies if the next hop cannot accept the extension.
  • Charsets other than UTF-8 are prohibited in mail addresses and message headers sent over the Internet.
  • When the local part has non-ASCII characters, using ASCII-compatible encoding in the domain part is discouraged, to keep processing consistent.

When local parts are internationalized, header fields SHOULD be in the fully internationalized form, using UTF-8 as the base character set. Header field names themselves stay in ASCII. If a server advertises both SMTPUTF8 and DSN, it MUST implement internationalized DSNs, including the ORCPT parameter.
sections.eli5: Sender and receiver first ask each other if they can handle the new letters. If the next stop cannot, the message is sent back instead of being scrambled.

sections.title: Downgrading and Legacy Systems
sections.content:
ASCII-only senders can always write to internationalized systems, since ASCII is a proper subset. The difficulty is the other way round. If the first-hop server does not support the extension, originating systems SHOULD be ready to send conventional envelopes and headers, or return the message so it can be downgraded manually, possibly with encoded words. That requires ASCII-only addresses for all senders and recipients.

The RFC says downgrading cannot happen in transit. RFC 5321 requires that the local part MUST be interpreted and assigned semantics only by the host named in the domain part, because intermediate hosts that modified it caused long-standing problems. A downgrade that rewrites the local part can therefore only be applied at the endpoints: the user agent or submission server, or the final delivery MTA.

After final delivery, the MTA MAY downgrade messages or mark them, but SHOULD keep a way to recover the original internationalized form without loss. The guidance on downgrading at submission and delivery is advice, not a normative requirement.
sections.eli5: If a friend's mail program cannot read the new letters, the best time to switch to plain letters is at the start or the very end of the trip, not by a stranger halfway.

sections.title: Lessons from the Experimental Protocols
sections.content:
The earlier experimental set, described in RFC 4952, supported in-transit downgrading. It essentially required each non-ASCII address to be accompanied by an all-ASCII equivalent. That raised security concerns about pairing addresses that could not be authenticated, and an incompatible change to Internet mail addressing. The working group first judged the advantages worth these costs, but interoperability problems among initial implementations showed otherwise, and it moved ahead without in-transit downgrading.

As a result, RFC 5504 and RFC 5825 are described as irrelevant and no longer needed, and the RFC Editor was asked to move all three older documents to Historic.
sections.eli5: The first try had a clever trick that turned out to be too complicated and risky, so they dropped it and kept things simple.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
More permitted characters mean more risk. The same kind of homograph spoofing that affects internationalized domain names can affect the local part. A proposed fix of forcing displayed elements into normalized lowercase works for domain names in URLs but not for local parts, because those are case sensitive. Addresses copied from business cards and notes are also exposed to confusable characters, more so in very large mail systems where users pick their own addresses.

Downgrading mechanisms must not assume authenticated bindings between internationalized and ASCII addresses. Doing the transformations before final delivery, under the sending user's administrative control, reduces this risk. The RFC also warns that new forms of malformed message can enable attacks if a filter and a mail client interpret them differently.
sections.eli5: Some letters from different alphabets look the same, so a trickster could make a fake address that looks real. Everyone has to be careful about that.
